claims.text: The target materials are multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
The initial nanoparticles have a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Reducing nanoparticle size accelerates surface diffusion kinetics.
Faster surface diffusion causes element-specific segregation to begin earlier during heating.
Faster surface diffusion causes phase separation to begin earlier during heating.
Diffusion kinetics influence the high-temperature behavior of near-equiatomic multi-element alloys.
Surface defect density mediates surface diffusion kinetics.
Smaller nanoparticles have higher surface-to-volume ratios than larger nanoparticles.
A high surface-to-volume ratio enhances atomic mobility at elevated temperature.
Enhanced atomic mobility compromises homogeneous solid-solution stability through surface segregation and phase separation.
Smaller nanoparticles will exhibit segregation or secondary phases at lower onset temperatures than larger nanoparticles under otherwise identical conditions.
Smaller nanoparticles will exhibit segregation or secondary phases after shorter heating times than larger nanoparticles.
Uncoated nanoparticles will segregate or form secondary phases earlier than surface-capped nanoparticles.
Stabilizing surface coatings maintain a lower surface-to-volume ratio.
Stabilizing surface coatings delay or reduce segregation during thermal exposure.
The proposed size-mediated effect applies across 773–1173 K for catalytic operation and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric operation.
The proposed effect applies under inert, reducing, and oxidizing atmospheres.
The mechanism may not apply to compositions far from equiatomic ratios or at temperatures substantially outside the specified ranges.

contradictions.description: The intervention treats surface capping as a surface-characteristic variable, whereas the baseline attributes capping to a lower surface-to-volume ratio. At fixed particle size, adding a cap does not constitute the same geometric size change, so the stated baseline conflates geometric surface-to-volume ratio with surface stabilization.
